2. Both the IT Reference Applications were filed by the Commissioner of Taxes, Tax Zone -2, Chittagong. The IT Reference application No. 102 of 2005 arose against an order of the Taxes Appellate Tribunal Chittagong, Chittagong (Circuit Bench) passed in ITA No. 828 of 2003-2004 and ITA No. 1528 of 2003-2004 ( Assessment years 2002-2003) dated 10.01.2004 and the Assessee-Respondent in this case is Md. Safi of 1403 Sheikh Mojib Road, Chittagong. The IT Reference Application No. 104 of 2005 arose against an order of the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Chittagong Bench, Chittagong (Circuit Bench) passed in ITA No. 982 of 2003-2004 ( Assessment Year 2002-2003) dated 10.01.2004 and the Assessee-Respondent in this case is P.H.P. Ship Breaking and re-cycling Industries Ltd. 

 "Whether on the facts and in the circumstance of the case  the Learned Appellate Tribunal, Chittagong Bench, Chittagong was legally justified in confirming the Order in directing the DCT to make assessment under-Section 83 (2) of the IT Ordinance 1984 in place of Section 82C of the IT Ordinance 1984 by misinterpreting Section 82C" 

 11. Facts of the Cases: 

 The facts of the cases as has been stated in the instant IT Reference Applications are that the Assessee-Respondents submitted Income Tax returns for the assessment year 2002-2003 to the DCT  concerned, Company Circle- 8 Taxes Zone- 2, Chittagong on 20.10.2002 and 19.11.2002 in IT Reference Application No. 102 of 2005 and IT Reference Application No. 104 of 2005, respectively. In IT Reference Application No. 102 of 2005 the Assessee-Respondent submitted a revised Income Tax return to the same office for those years showing total income of Tk. 2,18,19,384.00 on 24.03.2003. 

 The learned DAG Mr. S. Rashed Jahangir, appearing on behalf of the Commissioner Applicant argued that the DCT concerned correctly and lawfully passed the assessment Order under Section 82C 2(c) and 83 (2) of the IT Ordinance 1984. The learned DAG tries to establish his contention by submitting that the Assessee-Respondents cases fall within the ambit of Section 82C (2)(c) of the ITO 1984 therefore, since they, the Assessee-Respondent's establishments are not "industrial undertakings" the Returns submitted by them were correctly and lawfully assessed hereunder. He further contends that they are importers for the purposes of Section 53 of IT Ordinance 1984 and Section 82 and particularly Sub-Section 2(c) of the said section, and therefore, they fall within the ambit of the said Sections, since the Assessee -Respondents inverted old ships and cut them into pieces and sold scrap plates and sold them in the local market. The Learned DAG tries to persuade that in the instant Cases the Assessee-Respondents did not undergo any industrial production process and further claimed by arguing that making scrap plates from scrap ships do not undergo any chemical, assembling or any other production process and therefore the Assessee-Respondents or their establishments cannot be described as an "industrial undertaking" since these establishments, ship-breaking concerns, do not possess the ingredients that may qualify them to fall under the definition and description of an "industrial undertaking". The Learned DAG in support of his contention also placed before us a circular issued by the National Board of Revenue dated 02.12.2000 wherefrom he tried to draw our focus upon inferring the fact that in order to be determined as an Industrial undertaking the importer has to pursuant to Ship Creaking, manufacture a separate new object through a manufacturing process. 

 15. The Learned Advocate Mr. Mosharraf Hossain while appearing for the Assessee-Respondents in both the Applications did not into any Affidavit-In-Opposition. He however, in course of the hearing made verbal submissions before the Court of which we have taken note of. The Learned Advocate appearing for the Assessee-Respondents argued that in the instant Cases, the concerned establishments, being ship-breaking concerns in both the Applications fall within the definition of an Industrial establishment and thereby engaged in a whole new manufacturing process which is an integral part and form the essence of an Industry. The Learned Advocate for the Assessee-Respondents also argued that the Commissioner of Taxes in preferring the Reference Applications against the Order of the Taxes Appellate Tribunal both dated 10.01.04 and the Orders of the AJCT dated 21.05.03 & 05.07.03 misinterpreted the Orders and also failed to comprehend and appreciate the legal reasoning behind those Orders. The Learned Advocate in support of his argument took as through the Learned AJCT's Orders dated 21.08.03 & Order dated 5.07.03 in Income Tax Reference Applications 102 of 2005 and IT Reference Application No. 104 of 2005 respectively. He contended that the Learned AJCT's Orders clearly state that the Assessee-Respondents establishments possess all the ingredients and fulfill the requisites of a manufacturing company and Industrial undertaking. He also relies on the Learned AJCT's factual findings that in the instant two cases, the Assess- Respondents after importing the Scrap Ships did not directly sell the ships in the local market. He further argued that on the contrary and as stated in the Order of A.ICT they dismantled the Ships and then in breaking and. converting them into scrap plates, which are "new objects" in every sense of the term and for all practical purposes. The Learned Advocate stressed upon the fact that they under went a whole manufacturing process and in the process of "manufacturing" the "scrap plates" used and consumed Electricity, Gas, Labors etc. and which are necessary and indispensable parts of an Industrial undertaking and to which value has been added for the purpose of VAT under the relevant Provision of VAT Act, 1991. 

 16. The Learned Advocate Mr. Mosharaf Hossain also drew our attention to the fact that as it apparent from the Learned AJCT's Order that Returns submitted in previous assessment years in similar cases and under similar circumstances by the Assessee-Respondent and by other concerns/ establishment doing and undergoing similar nature of business activities, were assessed under Section 83 (2) only of the IT Ordinance 1984 and they were not assessed under Section 82C of the Ordinance. He strenuously argued that therefore, it is clear that he has been under the circumstances, in the present nun cases, discriminated against by the Income Tax Authorities without any legal reasoning or lawful authority in having his Income Tax returns submitted under a different criteria and a different provision of law from that of the preceding returns previously submitted and assessed by the Income Tax Authorities. 

 19. In the instant cases the importer Assessee- Respondent's business concerns being 'ship-breaking' concerns, possess most of the ingredients required of an Industrial undertaking and in the process of manufacturing of "scrap plates" the Assessee- Respondents underwent the necessary requisites involving a manufacturing process and have used Electricity, Gas, Labor etc. which ingredients are indispensable for the running of an Industrial undertaking. Furthermore, it also appears from perusal of the records placed before us that further value have been also added to the manufacture of the goods. It also appears from the record that the Assessee-Respondents have not sold the imported scrap ship directly in the market. 

 22. From our perusal of documents and materials on record, our finding is that in the instant two Cases the Assessee- Respondents after importation of the said Scrap Ships did not directly sell the ships in the local market, rather in the contrary, they, the Assessee- Respondents dismantled the ships and thereby underwent a whole new manufacturing process using electricity, gas, labor etc and which are essential and indispensable parts of an industrial undertaking and furthermore, value was also added to those for the purpose of VAT under VAT Act, 1991. We are also of the opinion that through the process of converting "Scrap Ships" to "Scrap Plates" it can only be logically reasoned out that a "Scrap Ship" and a "Scrap Plate" are not the same objects and therefore we may come to the logical conclusion that a "Scrap Plate" is a new object and can only be used for a different purpose and therefore cannot be equated with the Scrap Ship, of which it was originally only a part of. Therefore, our understanding from the materials placed before us is that a "Scrap Plate" and a "Scrap Ship" are different objects meant for distinct and different use and can only be manufactured by an industrial under taking. 

 28. In this case the Applicant is on a misinterpretation and misconception of facts relying on Sub-section 2 (c) of Section 82C of IT Ordinance along with the non-obstante clause Sub-section 1 of the same Sections. The Applicant-Commissioner of Taxes in these Cases failed to appreciate the fact that Section 82C of IT 1984 or any part thereof is not applicable to the income of the Assessee-Respondents at all. It is evident that Section 82C (1) applies to those only, falling under the classification of persons coming within the ambit of Sub-section 2 of the said Section and the Assessce-Respondents do not come within any of the circumstances or the said ambit at all. Sub-section 2 (c) of Section 82C of the ITO 1984 infers the applicability of this Section to persons who are not "industrial Undertaking" within the meaning of the Section and the Scheme of the Ordinance and not to the Assessee-Respondents who are actually "Industrial Undertaking" under the IT Ordinance 1984. 

 30. From a plain reading of the above Section we are given to understand that the importers while importing the scrap ships shall pay Tax on account of import of goods. In these cases, the "goods" mean the Ships and as stated in Subsection 3 of Sections 53, the amount paid by the importer shall be thereby deemed to be an "advance payment of Tax." There is no conflict regarding the "Advance payment" of Tax and the Section also states that due to "Advance Payment" of 'Fax the importer shall be given the privilege of credit for during assessment. This pre-supposition of assessment subsequently entails and infers upon the fact that the total income of the Assessee is not assessed at this stage and his Tax liability are also certainly not over and Section 53 is applicable to the Assessce-Respondents since in their case, their Tax liabilities are not over at the import Stage and presuppose a subsequent assessment. 

 32. This section clearly states that in case of import of goods under section 53, the payment of Tax at the import stage shall be deemed to be final discharge of Tax liability. But our concern here is that the whole of such amount to be deemed as income of such person and the deeming of final discharge of Tax liability is applicable for establishments or concerns that are also "Industrial Undertaking" and according to our view, the Assesee-Respondents fall under the category of "industrial undertakings" and must be classified as such for the purposes of assessment of tax. 

 33. Therefore, we are inclined to apply our legal reasoning in these Two Cases and enunciate that the Assessee-Respondents are "Industrial Undertakings" consisting all the ingredients of Industries and therefore Section 53 is applicable to them and they shall be subject to advance payment of Tax presupposing a subsequent regular assessment or assessment at a later stage and certainly do not fall under the provisions of Section 82C or Section 82C (2)(c) and Section 82C (4) which presuppose the final discharge of Tax liability at the import stage and such situation do not apply and are not relevant for "Industrial Undertakings" and therefore are not applicable or relevant to the Assessee-Respondents in the present cases. 

 34. So far the Assessee-Respondents in these Cases are concerned they being "Industrial Undertakings", their Tax liabilities are not over and they shall pay only an advance payment of Tax and which they shall be given credit for during Assessment subsequently, whenever it takes place. 

 36. This circular has been referred to us by the Learned DAG and which was relied upon by him in defence of his contentions. The circular inter-alia, its short, states that Scrap Plates are not new objects and therefore ship breaking cannot be treated as an "Industrial Undertaking" since they are not producing new objects. The answer to this is not necessary to repeat since we have analyzed it quite extensively above. But we would also like to remind the Learned DAG relying on the "Circular" that this principle is a settled matter decided by our Apex Court that circulars do not have the force of law decided, inter-alia, in the case of Abul Basher -Vs- Bangladesh reported in 50 DLR, Appellate Division, Page-11. The relevant portion for our purpose is on page 12, Para 6 of the Judgment which is cited below. 

 41. We have also discovered from the materials placed before as and from the contention of the Learned Advocate representing the Assessee-Respondents that assessment of previous years of similar cases on similar issues involving the Assessor-Respondents and other enterprises and matters involved were assessed under Section 83(2) of the IT Ordinance only and not under Section 82C as is the case hereunder: 

 42. Therefore, it is difficult to conceive why the DCT concerned should treat these particular cases differently whereas similar cases involving similar issues in previous years were disposed of by assessment of returns under the Provisions of Section 83 (2) IT Ordinance 1984. This discrimination does not appear to be based on any legal or logical reasoning and can only be termed as arbitrary and upon complete misapplication of mind. 

 46. Moreover, a definition of industrial undertaking was inserted in F.A. 2005, and is presently Section 46A (1)(i) of the ITO. Though this case was filed some time before the insertion, we would like to city this definition for our understanding which is as under: 

 47. Therefore, the contention of the appellant that the Assessee-Respondent's establishments are not industrial undertakings does not stand on any legal footing and therefore the assessment of the DCT concerned in both the Cases we are dealing with instantly were unlawfully given and we are fully inclined to agree with the Orders given by the AJCT and the Learned Appellate Tribunal's Order. 

 48. Therefore, we conclude with the opinion that ship breaking is under the provision of the relevant laws recognized "industrial undertakings" possessing the ingredients of a manufacturing industry and therefore, Section 82C of the Ordinance or any part thereof is not at all applicable in the instant two cases.
